item.title: Wikimedia Files Amicus Brief Seeking Balanced AI Copyright Rulings
item.description:
Wikimedia Files Amicus Brief Seeking Balanced AI Copyright Rulings

The Wikimedia Foundation has filed an amicus brief in the high‑profile AI copyright lawsuits involving The New York Times, OpenAI and Microsoft. The nonprofit argues for a nuanced legal approach: training large‑language models (LLMs) on copyrighted content should be protected as fair use, while chatbots that directly reproduce that content to users should require a license.

🔍 Overview

  • Wikimedia filed the brief on Friday, weighing in on a set of lawsuits that pit major publishers against OpenAI and Microsoft.
  • The filing does not take a side for either the publishers or the AI companies; it instead pushes courts toward a middle ground.

⚖️ Legal Nuance

  • Training vs. Regurgitating: Using copyrighted material to train LLMs is presented as a transformative, fair‑use activity.
  • Output that Substitutes the Original: When an AI system pulls a passage and returns it to a user, effectively supplanting the original work, Wikimedia says that should require a license because the output is not sufficiently transformative.
  • Licensing Requirements: If AI companies use Wikipedia‑licensed content, they must credit the source and keep any remix or adaptation under the same Creative Commons license.

🤖 Impact on AI & Wikipedia

  • Benefits of LLMs for Wikipedia: The models can help editors detect vandalism, spot copyright violations, identify doxxing, and flag articles needing improvement.
  • Risks to the Community: AI services that scrape and reproduce Wikipedia content can siphon traffic away, weakening the volunteer community that maintains the site.
  • Potential Outcomes:
    • A publisher‑favored ruling could let copyright holders “gatekeep” even innovative uses of their work.
    • An AI‑favored ruling could become “a green light to snub licensing terms” and fragment knowledge flow.

💬 Wikimedia Leadership Statements

  • Stephen LaPorte (General Council): “A ruling that does not apply fair use principles carefully could threaten the sustainability of free knowledge, and stifle the development of open source technologies, ultimately impacting access to information for everyone in both cases.”
  • Bernadette Meehan (CEO): “We are taking a position in this case to defend the free and open human knowledge that Wikipedia depends on.”
  • The brief also notes that Wikipedia is created through a collaborative process that requires a strong foundation of open and accessible human knowledge.

📄 Key Points from the Brief

  • Wikimedia sites are “one of the most critical sources of data for all artificial intelligence and machine learning training.”
  • It alleges OpenAI infringed copyright by scraping Wikipedia to build training datasets.
  • OpenAI and Microsoft argue that LLM use is fair use; OpenAI calls regurgitation “a rare bug,” while Microsoft cites analysis showing Copilot rarely reproduces full sentences, “hardly undermines the transformative purpose of LLM training.”
  • The brief warns that a nuance‑free victory for either side could harm the open web and the future of free knowledge.

#Wikimedia #AIcopyright #LLM #OpenAI #Microsoft

Source: Wikipedia’s operator says a bad AI copyright ruling could threaten the open web

item.title: OpenAI Accuses Former Employee of Taking Confidential Files to Apple
item.description:
OpenAI Accuses Former Employee of Taking Confidential Files to Apple

OpenAI filed a new legal document alleging that a former employee who left to join Apple stole more than 100 confidential files containing its product plans and shared them with Apple leadership.

🔍 Overview

  • OpenAI’s filing, reported by Reuters, comes amid an ongoing legal battle with Apple over trade secrets.
  • The filing alleges the employee sent the stolen information to a personal account and then presented it to Apple executives, including the vice‑president of operations in Asia.
  • Apple has not responded to The Verge’s request for comment.

🧩 Accusations

  • The former employee took more than 100 confidential files before departing for Apple.
  • OpenAI says the employee “took its product plans and presented them to Apple.”
  • OpenAI is “very concerned that its trade secret and confidential information is now circulating inside Apple, where Apple engineers can shape Apple’s upcoming products based on OpenAI’s confidential and innovative work.”
  • Apple, in turn, accuses OpenAI of stealing confidential documents and spying on hardware prototypes.

📂 Confidential Files Allegedly Stolen

File Category Description
Images Pictures of at least one unreleased device
Supplier Information Details about component suppliers
Engineering Data Technical data related to hardware development
Project Files Internal project documentation
Cosmetic Finish Standards Guidelines for product appearance
Coating & Sealing Reports Reports about the “coating and sealing of hardware components”

📱 Apple’s New Devices Linked to the Leak

  • OpenAI links the former employee’s presentation to Apple’s new HomeView smart display and a range of other devices Apple revealed this week.
  • OpenAI notes that the presentation “appears to have happened months ago — and now, armed with that information, Apple is making a new push into AI‑enabled products.”
  • Apple’s smart display has been rumored for years, reflecting the long timeline typical of Apple’s product plans.

📣 Statements

  • OpenAI’s filing states: “OpenAI is very concerned that its trade secret and confidential information is now circulating inside Apple…"
  • Apple’s response: No comment provided to The Verge.

The information above reflects only what OpenAI and Apple have publicly alleged in the filing.

#OpenAI #Apple #TradeSecrets #Legal #AI

Source: OpenAI claims an ex-employee took its product plans and presented them to Apple

item.title: USA Today Sues OpenAI Over Alleged Unauthorized Use of News Articles
item.description:
USA Today Sues OpenAI Over Alleged Unauthorized Use of News Articles

USA Today Co has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging that the company used the publisher’s copyrighted articles without permission.

🏛️ Overview

  • The complaint states that OpenAI copied hundreds of thousands of articles and other materials belonging to USA Today Co for AI training.
  • The lawsuit seeks damages exceeding $250 million and an injunction to stop the alleged infringement.

📄 Claims and Demands

  • USA Today claims the material was used without permission.
  • The company is demanding over $250 million in damages and seeks a court order to prevent further use.
  • The complaint does not settle whether OpenAI is legally obligated to pay for any alleged use.

⚖️ Legal Issues

  • The central question is whether OpenAI’s use of the articles violates copyright or falls under fair use.
  • Fair use is a US copyright doctrine that permits use of copyrighted material without prior permission under certain conditions.
  • AI firms argue that training models is a fair‑use activity because the system learns patterns and generates new output.
  • Publishers dispute this, asserting that large‑scale copying should not be deemed legal.
  • Courts consider four factors:
    1. Purpose of the use
    2. Character of the copyrighted work
    3. Amount and substantiality of the portion used
    4. Effect on the market value of the original work
  • Additional considerations may include whether the use is sufficiently transformative, the commercial context, and the impact on the publisher’s ability to profit from its reporting.

📈 Potential Impact

  • The decision could shape how AI companies collect and use news articles in the future.
  • The case adds to a broader legal debate about applying existing copyright rules to generative AI.
  • Similar lawsuits have been filed by other news organizations, including The New York Times, against OpenAI and Microsoft.

📰 Industry Concerns

  • Publishers rely on revenue from advertisements, subscriptions, and licensing.
  • There is concern that AI products could use content without paying, potentially reducing publishers’ income.
  • AI‑generated answers might keep users from visiting the original news site, further impacting revenue.
  • Licensing agreements are presented as one way for AI developers to obtain commercial access to news content.

#OpenAI #CopyrightLaw #NewsIndustry #AIlitigation

Source: USA Today sues OpenAI: USA Today vs OpenAI: Key questions over ChatGPT training data, news copyright and whether publishers should be paid for their work - The Economic Times

item.title: USA Today Sues OpenAI for Over $250 Million Over Copyright Infringement
item.description:
USA Today Sues OpenAI for Over $250 Million Over Copyright Infringement

USA Today Co., together with several local newspapers it owns, has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI alleging that the AI company copied “hundreds of thousands” of articles to train its models.

🔍 Overview

  • USA Today is the latest publisher to sue OpenAI.
  • The lawsuit seeks damages of more than $250 million.
  • The filing claims OpenAI’s use of the content has caused “real and continuing” harm to the outlets.

⚖️ Legal Claims

  • OpenAI allegedly did not ask for permission to use USA Today’s articles.
  • The plaintiff asserts OpenAI “took” the content to build products worth hundreds of billions of dollars.
  • The complaint states that OpenAI’s commercial success rests on large‑scale copyright infringement.
  • The core allegation is that OpenAI copied hundreds of thousands of articles for training its AI models.

📄 Parties Involved

  • Plaintiff: USA Today Co. (including its local newspapers)
  • Local outlets named in the suit: The Tennessean, Indy Star, The Columbus Dispatch, The Oklahoman, and several others.
  • Other publishers currently suing OpenAI:
    • The New York Times
    • The Intercept
    • CNET owner Ziff Davis
    • CBC/Radio‑Canada
    • Encyclopaedia Britannica
    • Merriam‑Webster
    • The Seattle Times
    • A coalition of nearly 400 local newspapers

📈 Why It Matters

  • The case adds to a growing string of copyright lawsuits against OpenAI.
  • Plaintiffs argue that the alleged infringement harms the news industry’s ability to monetize content.
  • OpenAI has not responded to a request for comment from The Verge.

The outcome could influence how AI developers source and use copyrighted material.

#OpenAI #CopyrightLaw #MediaLawsuits

Source: USA Today becomes the latest publisher to sue OpenAI

item.title: AI Tools Challenge Trade Secret Protection, Says Legaltech Article
item.description:
AI Tools Challenge Trade Secret Protection, Says Legaltech Article

An article by intellectual property attorney Terry Wikberg in Legaltech News examines how artificial intelligence is reshaping trade secret protection and creating new risks for companies that rely on proprietary information.

🔍 Overview

  • The piece discusses the ways AI, especially large language models (LLMs), can threaten trade secrets.
  • It highlights the need for companies to reassess their secrecy measures in the AI era.

🧩 How AI Interacts with Trade Secrets

  • LLMs and other AI tools can aggregate, analyze, and infer information from public sources.
  • They can quickly reconstruct valuable trade secrets from seemingly unrelated disclosures such as marketing materials or conference presentations.

⚖️ Legal Implications

  • Trade secret owners may face heightened scrutiny of secrecy measures.
  • There is a growing role of AI‑assisted reverse engineering in uncovering protected information.
  • AI capabilities affect the “readily ascertainable” metric used in trade secret defenses.

💡 Recommendations for Businesses

  • Audit public disclosures to identify unintended exposure of proprietary data.
  • Strengthen internal controls around how confidential information is shared and stored.
  • Proactively evaluate trade secret protection strategies to address AI‑related risks.

READ: The Invisible Threat: How AI Can Threaten Trade Secret Protections (Subscription required)

#AI #TradeSecrets #IntellectualProperty

Source: The Invisible Threat: How AI Can Threaten Trade Secret Protections | Insights | Holland & Knight

item.title: Sony and Universal Music Group Sue Suno Over v6 Model Training
item.description:
Sony and Universal Music Group Sue Suno Over v6 Model Training

Sony and Universal Music Group (UMG) have filed a lawsuit against Suno, alleging that the company’s new v6 model infringes on their copyrights.

⚖️ Legal Allegations

Sony and UMG, who did not sign licensing agreements with Suno, accuse the company of “model laundering.” The labels argue that:

  • Training a new model on the outputs of an infringing model does not eliminate infringement.
  • Value from copied recordings is passed from infringing models into their outputs, and then into v6.
  • v6 is described in the complaint as “the fruit of the same poisoned tree.”
  • Even models not directly trained on the plaintiffs’ recordings benefit from Suno’s “retained unauthorized copies.”

⚙️ Technical Claims

Sony further alleges that Suno utilized distillation to train v6, claiming it was trained to replicate results from previous “teacher” models created using infringing data. The labels contend that Suno’s models will continue to be built on stolen data unless the company starts from scratch.

🔍 Suno’s Response

Regarding the development of v6, Suno representatives have stated the following:

  • Jack Brody told The Verge it was “trained from the ground up, with a new set of data,” which included “user data.”
  • Suno later confirmed to Engadget that this data includes “creations” from users.

#Suno #Copyright #MusicAI #Lawsuit

Source: Sony and UMG are suing Suno again
